title: What Is Eaten --- Wheat, Rice, Onion, Tomato, Honey

lessons.title: el trigo — the grain that got rubbed
lessons.gloss: the wheat — Latin triticum, the rubbed grain, from terere, to rub; trite is worn down the same way

segments.text: Before a new run: what two Latin words hide in sombra? (Sub and umbra.) And what was stella? (A star.)
el pan — what this becomes.
el agua — the other half of what bread needs.
TRI-go, stress on the first part. One tap for the r, and the g is hard before o. see reference.
el trigo — "the wheat."
Latin triticum, and that is built on terere, to rub or to wear away. Wheat was named for what you had to do to it: rub the grain out of the husk. The crop is named after the threshing, not the plant.

Terere wore a path through English too. Something trite has been rubbed smooth by overuse. Attrition is wearing down. Detritus is what has been rubbed off. Even detriment is a wearing-away, though it has gone abstract and stopped admitting it.
A useful habit, this: when a Latin food word looks odd, ask what was done to the food. The answer is often the whole etymology.
One word, and a small piece of the ancient working day.
You have had el pan for a long time. Now you have what it is made of, which means you can name a thing and the stuff it came from — a step up from naming things one at a time.

segments.instruction: el trigo, then el pan — the stuff, then the thing
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *el trigo*, then *el pan* — the stuff, then the thing]

segments.text: What did terere mean? (To rub.) Which English words still rub? (Trite, attrition, detritus.) And what is el trigo? (The wheat.)

lessons.title: el arroz — a word that brought its own article
lessons.gloss: the rice — Arabic ar-ruzz, carrying its own article; rice is the same grain by a different road

segments.text: Two back: what does la sombra name? (The shade.) And what did terere mean? (To rub.)
el trigo — the grain before this one.
el agua — what you cook it in.
a-RROZ, stress on the end. The rr at the start of the second part is the rolled one, held. see reference.
el arroz — "the rice."

This one did not come from Latin. Arabic ar-ruzz crossed into Spain with the crop itself, and Spanish took the phrase whole, article and all. Ar- was already "the." So el arroz says it twice, in two languages, and nobody minds.

Once you know to watch for it, that stuck-on a- is everywhere in the Arabic layer of Spanish: azúcar, aceite, almohada, aduana. Each one is still wearing an Arabic al- that Spanish stopped being able to see.
English got the same grain by a different road — Greek oryza, then Latin, then Italian, then French, arriving as rice. Same plant, two routes, and the words no longer look like relatives.
Two grains, and two completely different histories sitting side by side.

El trigo came down from Rome. El arroz came in from the south with farmers. That is Spanish in miniature: a Latin skeleton with a large Arabic vocabulary laid over the top, and the joins still visible when you know where to look.

segments.instruction: el trigo, then el arroz — Rome, then the south
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *el trigo*, then *el arroz* — Rome, then the south]

segments.instruction: arroz, azúcar, aceite — three words carrying an Arabic al-
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *arroz*, *azúcar*, *aceite* — three words carrying an Arabic *al-*]

segments.text: What does the ar- in arroz already mean? (The.) Name two more Spanish words carrying an Arabic article. (Azúcar, aceite, almohada.) And which English word is the same grain? (Rice.)

lessons.title: la cebolla — a little something, permanently
lessons.gloss: the onion — Latin caepulla, a little caepa; the chive in English is the same root, undiminished

segments.text: Before the new one: what does the ar- of arroz already mean? (The.) And what was triticum named for? (The rubbing, the threshing.)
comer — what you eventually do with it.
el arroz — what it usually goes into.
ce-BO-lla, stress in the middle. The c before e is soft, and the ll is close to an English y. see reference.
la cebolla — "the onion."
Latin had caepa for an onion, and caepulla for a small one. Spanish kept the small one and quietly dropped the full-sized word, so the language now calls every onion a little onion, however large.

That happens more than you would expect. A word with a diminutive on it gets used so often that the ending stops meaning anything, and the plain form falls away. You will meet the same -illa and -illo again shortly, still doing the job in words where it has not yet worn out.
English kept the other half. Chive came through French cive from that same caepa, and a chive really is a small one — so between the two languages the pair got split down the middle.
Three things you can put in a pot, and a piece of machinery worth more than the three.
El trigo, el arroz, la cebolla. Hearing a small ending as "a little one of these" will unlock words you have not been taught, which is the whole point of taking them apart.

segments.instruction: el trigo, el arroz, la cebolla

segments.text: What was caepa? (An onion.) What did caepulla add? (Smallness.) Which English plant is the same root? (Chive.)

lessons.title: el tomate — a word that came the other way
lessons.gloss: the tomato — Nahuatl tomatl, one of the words Spanish carried back across the Atlantic

segments.text: Quick pass: what was caepa? (An onion.) What does ar- mean in arroz? (The.) And what is el trigo? (The wheat.)
la cebolla — what it is usually cooked with.
rojo — what colour it goes.
to-MA-te, stress in the middle. Three clean vowels, none of them swallowed. see reference.
el tomate — "the tomato."

Take this one apart and nothing Latin falls out, because there is nothing Latin in it. Tomatl is Nahuatl, the language of the Mexica, and the plant and its name travelled to Spain together in the sixteenth century.

Spanish shaved the -tl into -te, which is what it did to the whole set: chocolatl became chocolate, ahuacatl became aguacate, coyotl became coyote. Then English took them from Spanish, which is why an English speaker already owns three Nahuatl words without knowing it.
So the traffic ran both ways. Spanish handed sombrero to English and took tomate from Mexico, and both words now sit in the same everyday vocabulary with no label saying where they have been.
Four foods, and three separate continents behind them.
El trigo is Roman. El arroz is Arabic. El tomate is American. One short set of words, and the history of who fed whom is sitting inside it.

segments.instruction: tomate, chocolate, aguacate — the same ending three times
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *tomate*, *chocolate*, *aguacate* — the same ending three times]

segments.instruction: el arroz con tomate y cebolla
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *el arroz con tomate y cebolla*]

segments.text: What language is tomate from? (Nahuatl.) What happened to the -tl ending? (It became -te.) Name two more words that did it. (Chocolate, aguacate, coyote.)

lessons.title: la miel — the sweetness inside three English words
lessons.gloss: the honey — Latin mel, which sweetens mellifluous, molasses and marmalade

segments.text: Before the last of the five: what language gave us tomate? (Nahuatl.) What was caepa? (An onion.) And what does ar- mean? (The.)
el pan — what you put it on.
la flor — where it starts.
MIEL, one beat. The ie is a single slide, and the l is bright, never the dark English one at the end of a word. see reference.
la miel — "the honey."
Latin mel, four letters shorter than most of what we have taken apart, and Spanish did little to it beyond breaking the e into ie — the same break you met in cielo.

Mel is sweeter in English than it looks. Something mellifluous flows with honey, which is what fluere is doing on the end of it. Molasses came through Portuguese melaço, the honey-like leavings of sugar. And marmalade carries the Greek form meli, stuck to melon, quince — a quince-honey, which is exactly what marmalade is.
There is a lesson hidden in that last one. A word can be perfectly transparent in its own language and completely opaque once it has crossed two borders.
Five: el trigo, el arroz, la cebolla, el tomate, la miel.

Set out together they are a shopping list, and they are also four separate histories — Rome, Arabia, Mexico, and Rome again. Every one of the five arrived with an English relative attached, which is the quiet argument this whole approach rests on: you know more of this language than you have been taught.

segments.instruction: all five — el trigo, el arroz, la cebolla, el tomate, la miel
segments.source: [YOU SAY: all five — *el trigo*, *el arroz*, *la cebolla*, *el tomate*, *la miel*]

segments.text: What was mel? (Honey.) What does mellifluous say, taken apart? (Flowing with honey.) And which breakfast preserve is a quince-honey? (Marmalade.)
